column1: #tags column:3
Define current and its unit; what does a negative current mean?
column2: i = dq/dt, in amperes (1 A = 1 C/s ≈ 6.24×10^18 elementary charges per second). Negative means the flow is opposite to the chosen reference arrow.

column1: Define voltage and its unit.
column2: Energy per unit charge between two points, v_AB = v_A − v_B = dw/dq, in volts (1 V = 1 J/C). Always between two points; a node voltage is relative to the reference node.

column1: State the three conditions of the lumped matter discipline.
column2: (1) No changing magnetic flux links any loop outside the elements; (2) no net charge accumulates inside an element (or node); (3) signals change slowly compared with the time waves take to cross the circuit.

column1: Which lumped condition gives KCL, and which gives KVL?
column2: Nodes store no charge (condition 2) plus charge conservation give KCL. No changing flux outside elements (condition 1) plus Faraday's law make ∮E·dl = 0, giving KVL.

column1: Passive sign convention: statement and consequence.
column2: Reference the current INTO the + terminal; then p = vi is the power ABSORBED. Negative p means the element delivers power.

column1: Why does SPICE report a negative current for a battery that is discharging?
column2: SPICE uses the passive convention for sources too: current is positive into the + terminal. A delivering source pushes current out of its + terminal, so it reads negative, and its @V[p] is negative.

column1: State Tellegen's theorem and why it holds.
column2: Σ v_k i_k = 0 over all branches (passive convention). Write v_k as node-voltage differences (KVL) and regroup by node; each node's currents sum to zero (KCL). No element laws used, so it holds for any lumped circuit.

column1: Lumped rule of thumb for digital edges, and the delay of FR-4 stripline?
column2: Lumped if one-way delay t_d < t_r/6. FR-4 stripline (εr ≈ 4.6): about 7.15 ps/mm, so 1 ns edges allow about 23 mm.

column1: Is mAh energy? Convert 225 mAh at 3.0 V.
column2: No: mAh is charge (1 mAh = 3.6 C). Energy = charge × voltage: 0.225 Ah × 3.0 V = 0.675 Wh = 2430 J.

column1: Average current of a duty-cycled device?
column2: I_avg = Σ D_k I_k (duty cycle × current for each activity, plus the always-on sleep current). Battery life = capacity / I_avg. A huge current at a tiny duty cycle can be a small share.

column1: Why is average power not V_avg × I_avg?
column2: P_avg is the average of v(t)·i(t); it depends on when v and i are large together. Only at DC (or with one factor constant) does it equal the product of averages.

column1: Distribution loss for power P at voltage V through resistance R?
column2: I = P/V, so loss = P²R/V² and loss fraction = PR/V². Doubling V quarters the loss; for equal loss the copper area can shrink by the square of the voltage ratio.

column1: Efficiency of a chain of converters?
column2: η_total = η_1 × η_2 × … ; loss = P_out(1/η − 1). Example: 97% × 90% = 87.3%, so 1 kW out needs 1145.5 W in.

column1: How much current does a 1 kW chip draw at 0.8 V, and what path resistance keeps the drop under 2%?
column2: 1250 A; 2% of 0.8 V = 16 mV, so R ≤ 16 mV / 1250 A = 12.8 µΩ. Hence regulators sit next to, under or inside the package.

column1: Ohm's law: forms, units and the sign condition.
column2: v = Ri, i = Gv, G = 1/R; ohm = V/A, siemens = A/V. Holds as written with the passive sign convention; with the current arrow out of the + terminal it is v = −Ri.

column1: Three forms of resistor power, and which resistor dissipates more in series and in parallel?
column2: p = vi = i²R = v²/R ≥ 0. In series (same i) the larger R dissipates more; in parallel (same v) the smaller R dissipates more.

column1: Sheet resistance and squares.
column2: R_□ = ρ/t (Ω per square); R = R_□ × L/W. A square of any size has R_□. 1 oz PCB copper (35 µm) ≈ 0.49 mΩ/□.

column1: Copper's resistivity and temperature coefficient (IACS).
column2: 1.7241 µΩ·cm at 20 °C (17.2 mΩ per meter per mm²); +0.393 %/°C. A 65 °C rise adds about 26%.

column1: Element laws of short, open, ideal voltage source, ideal current source.
column2: Short: v = 0 for any i. Open: i = 0 for any v. Voltage source: v = v_s for any i (0 V source = short). Current source: i = i_s for any v (0 A source = open).

column1: Which ideal-source connections are impossible?
column2: Unequal voltage sources in parallel; a shorted voltage source; unequal current sources in series; an open current source. They violate KVL or KCL; real sources (with internal resistance) turn them into large currents.

column1: Practical source model and its two named points.
column2: v = V_oc − R_int i. Open-circuit voltage V_oc (i = 0); short-circuit current I_sc = V_oc/R_int (v = 0). Equivalent: I_sc in parallel with R_int.

column1: Find R_int from two load measurements.
column2: R_int = (V1 − V2)/(I2 − I1), the slope of the terminal line; then V_oc = V1 + I1 R_int. E.g. 3.90 V open, 3.75 V at 0.375 A → 0.40 Ω.

column1: Two cells of 4.20 V and 3.60 V, 50 mΩ each, in parallel: what happens?
column2: 6.0 A circulates (0.60 V / 0.10 Ω); terminal 3.90 V; 3.6 W of heat; the weak cell is charged. Never parallel unmatched cells.

column1: E-series: what E12, E24, E96 mean and their steps.
column2: n values per decade spaced ≈ 10^(1/n): E12 ≈ ×1.21 (±10%), E24 ≈ ×1.10 (±5%), E96 ≈ ×1.024 (±1%). IEC 60063. Several E12/E24 values (2.7, 3.3, 3.9, 4.7, 8.2…) are historical, not pure geometric.

column1: Thick-film versus thin-film chip resistors.
column2: Thick film: ±1–5%, ±100–200 ppm/K, cheapest, most common. Thin film: ±0.1–1%, ±10–50 ppm/K, about 10× better on both, at a premium.

column1: Worst-case analysis of an LED resistor current.
column2: Take each tolerance to the limit that pushes the output furthest: I_max = (V_s,max − V_LED)/R_min, I_min = (V_s,min − V_LED)/R_max. Supply variation acts on the small difference V_s − V_LED, so it often dominates.

column1: Static versus incremental resistance of a diode at 1 mA.
column2: Static v/i ≈ 0.6548 V / 1 mA = 655 Ω; incremental dv/di = V_T/I ≈ 25.9 Ω. Small signals see the incremental value.

column1: Why do the lowest-value shunts have worse TCR?
column2: The element alloy is low-TCR (<20 ppm/°C), but copper terminations (~3900 ppm/°C) become a larger share of a sub-milliohm total (an inference; one family goes from ±35 to ±350 ppm/°C).

column1: How many independent KCL and KVL equations does a circuit with n nodes and b branches have?
column2: n − 1 KCL (the n-th is implied) and b − n + 1 KVL (one per link of a spanning tree; the meshes, for a planar circuit). Total b, to pair with b element laws.

column1: Series and parallel resistors: rules and two mental shortcuts.
column2: Series: R add, same current. Parallel: G add, same voltage; R1∥R2 = R1R2/(R1+R2). N equal in parallel = R/N; parallel result < smallest resistor.

column1: Voltage divider and current divider formulas (two resistors).
column2: Voltage: v2 = v R2/(R1 + R2). Current: i1 = i R2/(R1 + R2), the crossover: the smaller resistor takes the larger current.

column1: Loaded divider: output and error.
column2: v_out = v_in (R2∥RL)/(R1 + R2∥RL). Divider looks like a source of R1∥R2; error ≈ (R1∥R2)/RL: 10× load ≈ 9%, 100× ≈ 1%, 1000× ≈ 0.1%.

column1: Why is a divider's ratio error up to twice each resistor's tolerance?
column2: The output depends on R1/R2; the worst case moves them in opposite directions, so the ratio error approaches the sum of the tolerances (1%+1% → ~2%). Matched networks track and do far better.

column1: Wheatstone bridge output and balance.
column2: v_out = V[R2/(R1+R2) − R4/(R3+R4)]; balanced (0) when R1R4 = R2R3. At balance the excitation drops out.

column1: Quarter-, half- and full-bridge outputs for a small ΔR/R.
column2: Quarter ≈ (V/4)(ΔR/R), nonlinearity ≈ ΔR/(2R). Half (equal and opposite) = (V/2)(ΔR/R), linear. Full = V(ΔR/R), linear, with temperature cancellation.

column1: Strain gauge: gauge factor and the size of the signal.
column2: ΔR/R = GF·ε, GF ≈ 2 for foil. 1000 µε → 0.2%; a 2.5 V quarter bridge gives about 1.25 mV, so bridges feed instrumentation amplifiers.

column1: Delta-to-wye and wye-to-delta formulas.
column2: Δ→Y: R_a = R_ab R_ca / (R_ab + R_bc + R_ca) (the two touching a, over the sum). Y→Δ: R_ab = (R_aR_b + R_bR_c + R_cR_a)/R_c (over the opposite one). Equal: R_Y = R_Δ/3.

column1: R–2R ladder: why only two values?
column2: Looking onward from every node is 2R∥2R = R, so current halves at each rung: binary-weighted currents from R and 2R only; accuracy depends on the R:2R ratio, easy to match on a chip.

column1: Why do node voltages satisfy KVL automatically?
column2: Each branch voltage is v_a − v_b. Around any loop every node voltage is added once and subtracted once, so the sum is identically zero; only KCL (n − 1 equations) remains.

column1: Write the nodal matrix G by inspection.
column2: G_kk = sum of all conductances touching node k (including to ground); G_kj = −(conductance between k and j); i_k = source current pushed into node k. G·v = i.

column1: Three properties of G for resistors and independent sources, and why.
column2: Symmetric (a resistor appears in both nodes' rows); diagonally dominant (diagonal holds every conductance at the node); positive definite if every node has a path to ground (vᵀGv = Σ G(v_a − v_b)² = power).

column1: Grounded versus floating voltage source in nodal analysis.
column2: Grounded: fixes a node voltage, drop that node's KCL, move V_s to the neighbours' right sides. Floating: supernode around the source and both nodes (its current cancels) plus the constraint v_a − v_b = V_s.

column1: What does MNA add to nodal analysis?
column2: One unknown per voltage source (its current, into the + terminal) and one constraint row v_a − v_b = V_s: [[G, B], [Bᵀ, 0]]·[v; j] = [i; e]. Symmetric but not positive definite (zero block), so LU with pivoting.

column1: Resistor, current-source and voltage-source stamps.
column2: R between a, b: +G at (a,a), (b,b); −G at (a,b), (b,a). I into node a: +I at row a (−I at row b). V (+ at a, − at b): +1 at (a,m), (m,a); −1 at (b,m), (m,b); V at row m.

column1: Why does SPICE report a negative current for a battery that delivers power?
column2: MNA's source-current unknown is defined into the + terminal (passive convention). A delivering source pushes current out of its + terminal, so the reported current is negative.

column1: A SPICE run fails with a singular matrix. Two likely causes?
column2: A node with no DC path to ground (only capacitors, or a floating subcircuit: G has a zero eigenvalue) or a loop of ideal voltage sources. Fix: add the missing path, e.g. a large resistor.

column1: Companion model of a diode at a Newton iterate v_k.
column2: Conductance g = f′(v_k) in parallel with current source I_eq = f(v_k) − g·v_k; stamp both, solve the linear circuit, repeat. Each Newton step is one sparse linear solve.

column1: How sparse is an N × N power-grid matrix?
column2: N² + 4N(N − 1) ≈ 5N² nonzeros out of N⁴. N = 100: 49,600 of 10⁸ (0.05%); dense storage 800 MB versus about 0.6 MB sparse. Dense LU at N = 1000 would need 8 TB.

column1: Static IR drop: what sets it and what fixes it?
column2: Current × resistance along the path from the bumps; worst at the point farthest from every bump. Fixes: more and better-placed bumps, wider or thicker metal, backside power. Dynamic drop (switching) is usually worse.

column1: Vendor claims 'billion-element simulation'. What do you ask?
column2: Which tool (FastSPICE partitions and simplifies models), what accuracy versus true SPICE on the same block, on which circuits, cores and versions. Speed-ups are best-case and design-dependent.

column1: Why do mesh currents satisfy KCL automatically?
column2: Each mesh current circulates around a closed loop: it enters every node it visits along one branch and leaves along another, so its net contribution at every node is zero. Only KVL (b − n + 1 equations) remains.

column1: Write the mesh matrix R by inspection (all meshes clockwise).
column2: R_kk = total resistance around mesh k; R_kj = −(resistance shared by meshes k and j); v_k = sum of source rises met going around mesh k in its direction. R·i = v.

column1: Current source on an outer branch versus shared by two meshes.
column2: Outer: it fixes that mesh current (i_k = ±I_s); drop that mesh's KVL. Shared: supermesh, KVL around both meshes avoiding the source, plus the constraint i_a − i_b = ±I_s.

column1: How many unknowns: nodal versus mesh?
column2: Nodal: (n − 1) − (number of voltage sources). Mesh: (b − n + 1) − (number of current sources). Parallel-heavy circuits favour nodal; series-heavy, few-loop circuits with current sources favour mesh.

column1: When can you not use mesh analysis, and what replaces it?
column2: When the circuit is nonplanar (contains K3,3 or K5): it has no meshes. Use loop analysis on the fundamental loops of a spanning tree (one per link), or nodal analysis.

column1: Why do simulators use nodal rather than mesh analysis?
column2: A netlist gives each element's two nodes, so nodal stamps are immediate; meshes need a planar embedding (impossible for nonplanar circuits) or a tree search. Nagel's SPICE2 found MNA needed substantially less computation.

column1: The dual of a planar circuit.
column2: Mesh → node, KVL → KCL, R (Ω) → G (S, same number), voltage source → current source, series → parallel, short → open, supermesh → supernode. The dual's node voltages equal the original's mesh currents.

column1: Why is the mesh matrix positive definite?
column2: iᵀRi = Σ R_b i_b², the resistor power. It is zero only if every resistor carries no current, which forces i = 0 unless a loop is made entirely of ideal voltage sources and wires.

column1: Two batteries in parallel at 12.6 V and 12.0 V (50 mΩ and 80 mΩ). What happens?
column2: The stronger charges the weaker: with no load the circulating current is 0.6 V / 0.13 Ω ≈ 4.6 A. Parallel only matched cells, or isolate strings until their voltages agree.

column1: Common-impedance coupling: a 10 mΩ return shared with a 2 A motor.
column2: The sensor's ground sits R_g·I ≈ 20 mV above the supply's −: about 16 LSB of a 12-bit, 5 V ADC, and it moves with the motor. Fix: star ground (separate returns) or differential/Kelvin sensing.

column1: Resolution versus accuracy for a 16-bit ADC over 5 V.
column2: 1 LSB = 76.3 µV. A 20 mV ground offset is 262 LSB, so the bottom eight bits mean nothing. Ask for system-level error, not converter resolution.

column1: Resistance between opposite corners of a cube of 1 Ω resistors.
column2: By symmetry the current splits 1/3, 1/6, 1/3 along any path: 5/6 Ω. Adjacent corners 7/12 Ω, face diagonal 3/4 Ω (Foster: 12 × 7/12 = 7 = n − 1).

column1: The four dependent sources, their gain units and SPICE letters.
column2: VCVS v = μ v_x (V/V, E); VCCS i = g v_x (S, G); CCVS v = r i_x (Ω, H); CCCS i = β i_x (A/A, F). F and H are controlled by the current through a named voltage source.

column1: Nodal analysis with dependent sources: the extra step.
column2: Write KCL treating the dependent source as known, then express its controlling variable in node voltages and move it to the left side. The matrix is then generally not symmetric.

column1: Why is G not symmetric with a VCCS?
column2: A VCCS g(v_c − v_d) driving node a adds +g at (row a, column c) but nothing at (row c, column a): the control affects the output, not the reverse.

column1: Finding a Thévenin resistance with dependent sources.
column2: Turn off independent sources only; keep dependent sources; apply a test source v_t (or i_t) and compute R = v_t/i_t. Series-parallel reduction does not work.

column1: Resistance seen into a bipolar base with emitter resistor R_E.
column2: r_π + (β + 1)R_E: the base current produces an emitter current (β + 1) times larger. 100 Ω at β = 100 looks like 10.1 kΩ.

column1: The Miller effect for a resistor.
column2: R_f from input to output of an amplifier with gain μ looks like R_f/(1 − μ) from the input: R_f/(1 + A) for inverting gain −A; infinite at μ = 1 (bootstrapping); negative for μ > 1.

column1: MOSFET small-signal model and intrinsic gain.
column2: VCCS g_m v_gs from drain to source in parallel with r_o; gate draws no current. Intrinsic gain g_m r_o is the most one transistor can give; common-source gain −g_m(r_o ∥ R_D ∥ R_L).

column1: Bipolar small-signal model and its numbers at 1 mA.
column2: r_π from base to emitter, CCCS β i_b (equivalently g_m v_be) from collector to emitter. g_m = I_C/V_T = 38.7 mS at 1 mA; r_π = β/g_m = 2.59 kΩ at β = 100.

column1: Source degeneration: gain and why use it.
column2: Gain −g_m R_D/(1 + g_m R_S) ≈ −R_D/(R_S + 1/g_m). Lower gain but set by resistors, less sensitive to g_m or β, more linear: the simplest negative feedback.

column1: Closed-loop gain of a non-inverting amplifier with finite op-amp gain A.
column2: A/(1 + Aβ) with β = R_1/(R_1 + R_2); relative error ≈ 1/(Aβ). A = 10⁵, gain 10: about 100 ppm. Error falls one decade per decade of A.

column1: Output resistance of a degenerated MOSFET.
column2: R_out = R_S + r_o(1 + g_m R_S): the VCCS resists changes in current, multiplying r_o. The principle of the cascode; it matters because a current source's accuracy is ΔV/r_o.

column1: What can go wrong when a dependent-source loop has gain near 1?
column2: The circuit matrix approaches singularity: huge sensitivity, negative resistance, and with capacitance present oscillation or latch-up. Small-signal models also ignore supply rails and saturation.

column1: The two properties of a linear system.
column2: Homogeneity, f(ax) = a f(x), and additivity, f(x₁ + x₂) = f(x₁) + f(x₂). R, dependent sources, C and L are linear; diodes and transistors (beyond small signals) are not.

column1: Why is every response of a linear circuit a weighted sum of its sources?
column2: MNA: A x = z with A built from linear elements only, and z = Σ s_j b_j. So x = Σ s_j (A⁻¹ b_j). Fails when A depends on the solution (nonlinear elements).

column1: Superposition: how to switch off sources.
column2: Voltage source → short (0 V); current source → open (0 A). Dependent sources are never switched off. Solve each sub-circuit and add with signs.

column1: Why does power not superpose?
column2: p = R(i′ + i″)² = Ri′² + Ri″² + 2Ri′i″. The cross term can dominate: two sources can drive equal and opposite currents through a resistor (true power 0).

column1: When do average powers add?
column2: When the cross term averages to zero: signals at different frequencies (including DC plus AC) and independent zero-mean noise. That is why noise powers add (RSS of RMS values).

column1: Source transformation and Millman's theorem.
column2: V_s in series with R ⇔ V_s/R in parallel with R (terminal equivalence only). Parallel practical sources: V = Σ(V_k/R_k)/Σ(1/R_k), R = (Σ1/R_k)⁻¹.

column1: Unit-output method on a ladder of equal resistors.
column2: Assume 1 V out and work back: node voltages and currents are Fibonacci numbers (1, 2, 5; 1, 3, 8): three sections give 1/13. Input resistance → 1.618R for a long ladder.

column1: Worst case versus RSS in an error budget.
column2: Worst case Σ|e_k|: a hard bound. RSS √Σe_k²: valid for independent random errors and meaningful at a stated confidence only if each e_k is at that level (uniform limits: RSS ≈ 1.7σ, exceeded by ~7%).

column1: Why is a DAC's DNL worst at the major carry?
column2: At 011…1 → 100…0 the MSB switches in while every lower bit switches out, so any error of the MSB weight relative to the sum of the others shows up as a wrong step there.

column1: Superposition with a diode: when does it work?
column2: Not for large signals (1 mA + 5 V sources: superposed 1.32 V versus true 0.70 V). It works for small changes about an operating point using the small-signal model (r_d = V_T/I_D).

column1: State Thévenin's and Norton's theorems.
column2: A linear two-terminal network ≡ V_th (open-circuit voltage) in series with R_th, or I_N (short-circuit current) in parallel with R_th. V_th = R_th I_N; R_th = v_oc/i_sc.

column1: How does superposition prove Thévenin's theorem?
column2: Drive the terminals with a current i. Internal sources alone give v_oc; i alone (sources off) gives −R_th i by homogeneity. So v = v_oc − R_th i for any load, linear or not.

column1: Three ways to find R_th.
column2: (1) v_oc/i_sc; (2) switch off independent sources and combine resistors (no dependent sources only); (3) test source with dependent sources kept (needed when the network has dependent sources).

column1: Loading rule of thumb.
column2: Voltage interface: R_L ≫ R_th, error ≈ R_th/R_L (1 kΩ into 1 MΩ: 0.1%). Current interface: R_L ≪ R_th.

column1: What does a Thévenin equivalent not tell you?
column2: Anything inside: internal power, efficiency, heating. Thévenin and Norton forms of one network dissipate different amounts internally. It also needs the network (not the load) to be linear.

column1: PoE Type 4 as a Thévenin source.
column2: 52 V minimum behind 6.25 Ω (100 m, 4 pairs): 90 W at the PSE is 1.73 A, the cable drops 10.8 V and wastes 18.7 W, leaving 71.3 W at the device. Max V²/4R = 108 W, but only at 26 V.

column1: Why did 802.3bt power all four pairs?
column2: Two pairsets in parallel halve the loop resistance (12.5 → 6.25 Ω), halving cable loss at a given current, which together with 52 V minimum lets Type 4 deliver 71.3 W versus 25.5 W for 802.3at.

column1: Two-load method and the meter.
column2: 1/v = 1/V_th + (R_th/V_th)(1/R_L): two readings give a line. Include the meter's resistance in each load: a 10 MΩ meter on a 200 MΩ source reads under 5% of the true voltage.

column1: Constant-power load on a Thévenin source.
column2: v² − V_th v + P R_th = 0: two solutions (the upper one is normal); none if P > V_th²/(4R_th): the input voltage collapses (undervoltage lockout).

column1: Output resistance of an emitter follower.
column2: R_E ∥ (R_s + r_π)/(β + 1): base-side resistance divided by β + 1 (about 1/g_m plus R_s/β). β = 100, r_π = 2.5k, R_s = 1k: about 33 Ω.

column1: Maximum power transfer: condition, power, efficiency.
column2: R_L = R_th (load voltage V_th/2); p_max = V_th²/(4R_th); efficiency 50% if R_th is a physical series resistance (not for a general network). Loads R_th/k and kR_th get the same power; a factor 2 off keeps 89%.

column1: The power–efficiency tradeoff.
column2: p/p_max = 4η(1 − η) for a voltage behind a physical series resistance (battery, cable): 95% efficient gives 19% of max power; 99% gives 4%. A general network's Thévenin model does not give its internal loss.

column1: Should a power supply's output resistance equal its load?
column2: No. The theorem chooses a load for a given source. If you design the source, make R_th as small as possible: more power, less waste, better regulation.

column1: When do engineers match?
column2: Given sources with scarce power (antennas, sensors, harvesters) and transmission lines (to avoid reflections, load = Z0). AC form: conjugate match Z_L = Z_th*.

column1: Why 50 Ω?
column2: Air coax: minimum conductor loss at b/a = 3.59 (77 Ω); maximum peak power at b/a = √e (30 Ω). 50 Ω compromises (10% extra loss, 86% of max power); with PE dielectric min loss is 51 Ω. 75 Ω (video) favors loss in air or foam cable; with solid PE, 50 Ω is the low-loss choice.

column1: MPPT for a TEG versus a solar cell.
column2: TEG (linear source): maximum power at V_oc/2, and a fixed matched resistor tracks it. Solar cell (diode curve): MPP near 80–85% of V_oc; trackers find it by perturb and observe.

column1: Battery at maximum power: why never?
column2: 12 V, 0.1 Ω: 360 W into 0.1 Ω at 60 A and 50% efficiency (360 W of internal heat). At 95% efficiency (1.9 Ω): 68 W at 6 A with 3.6 W of loss.

column1: Maximum power with a negative source resistance?
column2: None: p = V²R_L/(R_L + R_th)² has a pole at R_L = −R_th. A real circuit saturates or oscillates; V²/4R_th is meaningless.

column1: The two ideal op-amp rules, and when they hold.
column2: 1) No current into either input. 2) Virtual short v+ = v−. Rule 2 holds only with negative feedback and the output inside its range; a saturated output breaks it.

column1: Inverting versus non-inverting gain and input resistance.
column2: Inverting: −R2/R1, input resistance R1 (virtual ground). Non-inverting: 1 + R2/R1, input resistance essentially infinite. Both have noise gain 1 + R2/R1.

column1: What is the noise gain and why does it matter?
column2: 1 + R2/R1, the gain from the + input to the output. Offset voltage and input noise see it in every configuration, and the finite-gain error is about (noise gain)/A.

column1: Difference amplifier output, and its CMRR with tolerance t.
column2: v_out = G(v2 − v1) if R4/R3 = R2/R1 = G. A_cm = (b − a)/(1 + b); worst-case CMRR ≈ (1 + G)/(4t): 1% and G = 100 give about 68 dB.

column1: Three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier gain, and why it beats a difference amp.
column2: G = (1 + 2R/R_G)(R2/R1). High input resistance on both inputs, one resistor sets gain, and the first stage passes common mode at gain 1, so CMRR is multiplied by the first-stage gain.

column1: Transimpedance amplifier: output and main DC error.
column2: v_out = −R_f i_in into a virtual ground (zero input resistance). Bias current adds I_B R_f: 250 nA × 500 kΩ = 125 mV, so large R_f needs picoamp-bias op-amps.

column1: Op-amp offset voltage: model and path to the output.
column2: A source V_OS in series with the + input, amplified by the noise gain. LM358: 3 mV typ, 7 mV max; OPA187 (zero-drift): 1 µV typ, 10 µV max at 25 °C.

column1: How do you cancel bias-current error?
column2: Make both inputs see the same resistance: put R1∥R2 in series with the + input of an inverting stage. The error drops from I_B R2 to I_OS R2.

column1: Error budget: sum of magnitudes or signed sum?
column2: Add magnitudes when signs are unknown (offset varies unit to unit). When physics fixes a sign (PNP inputs: both bias currents flow out) a signed sum is tighter: LM358 example 934.5 mV vs 984.5 mV.

column1: Choosing an op-amp for a 10 mV signal versus a 10 V signal.
column2: Compare offset with the error budget: for 10 mV at 0.1% (10 µV), only a zero-drift part works; for 10 V a 7 mV general-purpose offset is 0.07%. Choose by the size of the signal.

column1: Voltmeter loading error, and how to correct it.
column2: Reading = V_th R_in/(R_th + R_in): error ≈ −R_th/R_in. Correct with V_th = V_m(1 + R_th/R_in). A 10 MΩ meter on a 500 kΩ node reads 4.76% low.

column1: Ammeter burden: what it is and its error.
column2: The voltage the meter drops across its internal resistance R_A. The current falls by about R_A/R_th; correct with I_0 = I_m(1 + R_A/R_th). 1.8 Ω in a 33 Ω circuit: −5.2%.

column1: Read ±(0.05% + 1) for 0.300 V on a range with 1 mV resolution.
column2: 0.05% × 0.3 V + 1 mV = 1.15 mV = 0.38%: the count dominates. On the 0.1 mV range: 0.25 mV = 0.083%. Use the most sensitive range that does not overload.

column1: Resolution versus accuracy.
column2: Resolution: the smallest displayed step (one count). Accuracy: how far the reading may be from the truth, from the specification. Extra digits are not extra accuracy.

column1: Why four-wire (Kelvin) measurement works.
column2: Force leads carry the current (a current source ignores their resistance); sense leads attach at the element and carry almost no current, so they drop nothing. Removes leads and contacts; residual ≈ (R + R_s)/R_in.

column1: A shunt's sense traces tap the current-carrying copper. Consequence?
column2: Copper and solder between the taps add to the value (0.1 mΩ on 1 mΩ: +10%) and add copper's +0.39%/°C drift (585 ppm/°C effective in Example 06-11.5), which one-point calibration cannot remove.

column1: Shunt value tradeoff.
column2: Larger R: more signal, smaller relative amplifier offset, but I²R loss, heating and drift. Smaller R: less loss, but tiny signal and worse TCR at the lowest values. 10 mΩ at 5 A: 50 mV, 0.25 W.

column1: Remote sensing: what it does and costs.
column2: Sense wires from the load's terminals let the supply regulate there; its output rises by I(R_w+ + R_w−). Costs: two wires, headroom, cable loss unchanged. 12 V, 10 A, 39.5 mΩ: supply at 12.395 V.

column1: Copper wire and trace numbers to remember.
column2: ρ = 1.7241 µΩ·cm, +0.393%/°C (IACS, 20 °C). 1 oz copper: 35 µm, ≈ 0.49 mΩ/□. 16 AWG: 1.291 mm, 13.2 mΩ/m. Every 3 gauges halve the area.

column1: Three equal resistors across 9 V each read 2.81 V on a 10 MΩ meter. Is KVL broken?
column2: No. Each reading is taken with the meter loading that resistor (R_th = 667 kΩ), so each comes from a different circuit. Three meters connected at once would read 3 V each.
